experiments.title: Race Condition in Financial Counter
experiments.subtitle: Non-atomic read-modify-write corrupts transaction counters under concurrent load
experiments.scenario: A fraud detection service tracks per-merchant transaction counts in real time. Each incoming payment request increments a counter for the merchant ID. The service runs as a singleton Spring bean inside a high-throughput API gateway handling 50,000 requests per second. Counters are read every 10 seconds to trigger fraud alerts when thresholds are crossed.
experiments.impact: Under concurrent load, the non-atomic get-then-put sequence allows two threads to read the same stale counter value, both compute an increment, and write back — causing one increment to be silently lost. At peak load, counters can undercount by 10-30%, causing the fraud detection system to miss velocity thresholds and fail to block fraudulent merchants in time.
incorrectCode: private Map<String, Integer> counters = new HashMap<>();

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: HashMap is not thread-safe; concurrent structural modifications can corrupt the map or cause infinite loops
UNSAFE: get() reads a value that another thread may already have read and is about to overwrite
UNSAFE: increment computed on a stale value — another thread may have already incremented
UNSAFE: put() overwrites whatever any other thread may have written since the read on line 11

experiments.failureExplanation: HashMap provides no thread-safety guarantees. Two threads executing recordTransaction() concurrently can both read the same value (e.g., 42) on line 11, both compute newValue = 43, and both write 43 back — resulting in a net increment of 1 instead of 2. At high concurrency, this lost-update race can occur thousands of times per second. Additionally, concurrent structural modifications to HashMap (resizing) can cause data corruption or infinite get() loops.

simulation.title: Lost Update: Two Threads Increment the Same Counter

buggySteps.note: T1 reads current count = 42
⚠ T2 reads same stale value = 42
T1 computes newValue = 42 + 1 = 43
T2 computes newValue = 42 + 1 = 43 (also!)
T1 writes 43
⚠ LOST UPDATE: T2 overwrites with 43; should be 44!

simulation.bugAnnotation: Both threads read 42 before either writes back; one increment is permanently lost.

safeSteps.note: T1 calls counter.incrementAndGet() — atomic CAS loop

simulation.safeAnnotation: AtomicLong.incrementAndGet() is a single hardware CAS instruction; no lost updates possible.

experiments.correctExplanation: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent() atomically inserts a new AtomicLong if absent, and AtomicLong.incrementAndGet() uses a hardware CAS instruction to atomically read-modify-write the counter — eliminating both the data structure race and the lost-update race.

alternatives.name: LongAdder (high-contention stripe)
pros: Higher throughput under heavy write contention via cell striping
Avoids CAS retry spin under high concurrency
cons: sum() is not atomic — may return a slightly stale value if increments are concurrent
Higher memory footprint per counter due to cell array
alternatives.whenToUse: Use LongAdder when write throughput matters far more than read accuracy, such as metrics accumulators that are periodically drained.

experiments.performanceNotes: AtomicLong performs best when contention on a single counter is low to moderate; LongAdder achieves higher throughput under sustained high contention by distributing writes across CPU-local cells. For fraud counters with many distinct merchant IDs, AtomicLong is typically sufficient.

performanceTable.notes: Cell-striped; best for single hot counter

code: private final HashMap<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
tests.explanation: jcstress runs actor1 and actor2 concurrently and uses the arbiter to observe the final counter value. The FORBIDDEN outcomes assert that any result other than 2 (both increments preserved) indicates a lost-update bug — which jcstress will reliably reproduce on a multi-core machine.
tests.limitations: jcstress requires running with -jar jcstress.jar; it cannot be executed as a standard JUnit test. Results are sensitive to JVM warmup — run with at least 10,000 iterations for reliable detection.

monitoringSymptoms: Fraud alert rate drops or becomes inconsistent under peak load while raw transaction volume is stable
Merchant transaction counters show values lower than the sum reported by the upstream event log
Intermittent NullPointerException or ConcurrentModificationException in counter service logs
JVM thread dump shows multiple threads stuck in HashMap.get() resize loop
debugTips: Add a parallel exact counter using a synchronized baseline and compare periodically to detect undercount drift
Enable -verbose:gc and monitor HashMap resize events — concurrent resize is a strong signal of an unsynchronized shared map
Use async-profiler with wall-clock mode to find hot contentious paths in the counter service
productionRecommendations: Always use ConcurrentHashMap (never HashMap) for shared mutable state in singleton Spring beans
Prefer AtomicLong over synchronized Integer for single-value counters to avoid lock overhead
Instrument counters with Micrometer (Counter.builder) to get thread-safe metrics published to Prometheus without hand-rolling concurrency

assessment.text: Two threads call recordTransaction("merchant-99") simultaneously on a HashMap-backed counter currently at 100. What is the most likely outcome?
options: A) The counter will always reach 102 because Java ensures atomic map updates
B) The counter may end up at 101 due to a lost update race condition
C) A ConcurrentModificationException is always thrown
D) The counter will reach 102 but with a slight delay
assessment.explanation: Both threads read 100 before either writes, then both write 101, leaving the counter at 101 instead of 102. ConcurrentModificationException can occur but only during iteration, not simple get/put. Java makes no atomicity guarantees for HashMap operations.

assessment.text: Which replacement correctly fixes the race condition in recordTransaction()?
options: A) Wrapping the entire method body in a synchronized block on `this`
B) Using ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicLong> with computeIfAbsent + incrementAndGet()
C) Replacing HashMap with a TreeMap
D) Adding the volatile keyword to the counters field
assessment.explanation: ConcurrentHashMap provides thread-safe structural operations, and AtomicLong.incrementAndGet() is a hardware-level atomic CAS — eliminating both map-level and counter-level races. Synchronized works but serializes all merchants through one lock. TreeMap is not thread-safe. volatile only ensures visibility of the reference, not atomicity of the increment.

assessment.text: When should you prefer LongAdder over AtomicLong for a fraud counter?
options: A) When you need the most recent exact value at any instant
B) When many threads hammer the same single merchant counter simultaneously
C) When you have many distinct merchants with low per-merchant concurrency
D) When you need to persist the counter value to a database
assessment.explanation: LongAdder uses cell striping to reduce CAS contention — it shines when many threads contend on the exact same counter. For many distinct merchants with low per-merchant concurrency, AtomicLong is simpler and sufficient. LongAdder.sum() is also not point-in-time consistent, making it unsuitable when exact instantaneous reads are required.

experiments.title: Deadlock in Money Transfer
experiments.subtitle: Inconsistent lock acquisition order between two accounts causes circular wait
experiments.scenario: A core banking service processes money transfers between accounts. Each transfer acquires a lock on the source account and then on the target account before modifying balances. When two transfers run concurrently in opposite directions — Thread 1 transferring from Account A to Account B while Thread 2 transfers from Account B to Account A — each thread locks its source account first, then blocks waiting for the other's target account lock.
experiments.impact: Both threads block indefinitely, holding their locks and preventing all other transfers involving Account A or Account B. In production, this manifests as payment timeouts and customer-visible transaction failures. The deadlock can only be resolved by a timeout or application restart. If multiple account pairs are involved, deadlock can cascade and freeze the entire transfer processing pool.
incorrectCode: public void transfer(String fromId, String toId, BigDecimal amount) {

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: always acquires source lock first — ordering depends on caller, not on a canonical key order
UNSAFE: attempts to acquire target lock while holding source lock — if another thread holds target and wants source, deadlock occurs

experiments.failureExplanation: Thread 1 calls transfer("A", "B", ...) and acquires lock A, then blocks waiting for lock B. Thread 2 calls transfer("B", "A", ...) and acquires lock B, then blocks waiting for lock A. Neither thread can proceed — this is a classic circular wait (the fourth necessary condition for deadlock). Because synchronized blocks do not time out, both threads remain blocked indefinitely.

simulation.title: Deadlock: Circular Lock Wait on Account Locks

buggySteps.note: T1 acquires Lock-A (transfer source)
T2 acquires Lock-B (transfer source)
T1 waits for Lock-B (held by T2)
⚠ T2 waits for Lock-A (held by T1): DEADLOCK!

simulation.bugAnnotation: Circular wait: T1 holds Lock-A and wants Lock-B; T2 holds Lock-B and wants Lock-A. Neither can proceed.

safeSteps.note: T1 orders locks: compare(A,B) → acquire A first, then B
T2 orders locks: compare(B,A) → acquire A first, then B (same order!)

simulation.safeAnnotation: Lock ordering by account ID ensures all threads always acquire locks in the same global order — circular wait is impossible.

correctCode: public void transfer(String fromId, String toId, BigDecimal amount) {
experiments.correctExplanation: By comparing account IDs and always acquiring the lexicographically lower ID's lock first, all threads follow the same global lock ordering regardless of transfer direction — breaking the circular wait condition and making deadlock impossible.

alternatives.name: ReentrantLock with tryLock timeout
code: public void transfer(String fromId, String toId, BigDecimal amount)
pros: Deadlock cannot persist — tryLock times out and releases held locks
Works even when lock ordering by ID is not feasible
cons: Livelock is possible if two threads repeatedly collide at the same timeout interval — add jitter
More complex code with nested try/finally
Under high contention, timeout-and-retry adds latency
alternatives.whenToUse: Use tryLock when you cannot guarantee a canonical lock order (e.g., locks are created dynamically or IDs are not comparable), or when you need a bounded wait with a fallback.

experiments.performanceNotes: Lock-ordering with synchronized has zero overhead compared to the broken version — it only changes acquisition sequence. tryLock adds latency under contention due to retry loops; ensure jitter is added to avoid livelock. For read-heavy workloads, consider ReadWriteLock or optimistic locking.

performanceTable.notes: No contention overhead beyond lock serialization
Retry overhead; use jitter to avoid livelock
RDBMS handles ordering; suitable for persistent accounts

code: TransferService svc = new TransferService(/* in-memory setup */);
"Deadlock detected: transfers did not complete within 3 seconds");
tests.explanation: Two threads execute transfers in opposite directions simultaneously. If deadlock occurs, the CountDownLatch never reaches zero and await() returns false after 3 seconds, failing the assertion. If the fix is correct, both transfers complete and latch reaches zero.
tests.limitations: A 3-second timeout is a heuristic — a heavily loaded CI machine may occasionally time out without a true deadlock. Run with @RepeatedTest(50) to increase confidence.

monitoringSymptoms: Payment processing threads spike to max pool size and stay there while throughput drops to zero
JVM thread dump shows multiple BLOCKED threads forming a circular wait chain on account lock objects
Transfer latency p99 jumps from milliseconds to the HTTP timeout threshold (e.g., 30 seconds)
Deadlock detector alerts from APM tools (Datadog, New Relic) or JVM MXBean DeadlockedThreads count > 0
debugTips: Take a JVM thread dump (kill -3 or jstack) and look for BLOCKED threads — the deadlock cycle will be explicitly listed
Enable ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() on a background health-check thread to detect and alert on deadlock within seconds of occurrence
Add lock acquisition logging with thread name and account IDs to trace which transfers are involved
productionRecommendations: Always enforce a canonical lock acquisition order based on a stable key (account ID, UUID comparison) when acquiring multiple locks
Consider moving transfer logic to the database layer using SELECT FOR UPDATE in a single transaction — the RDBMS lock manager handles deadlock detection and retry automatically
Instrument lock wait times with Micrometer to detect increasing contention before it becomes a customer-visible outage

assessment.text: Thread 1 calls transfer("A", "B") and Thread 2 calls transfer("B", "A") simultaneously on the buggy implementation. What happens?
options: A) Both transfers complete successfully in the order they started
B) T1 acquires Lock-A, T2 acquires Lock-B, and both block forever waiting for the other's lock
C) Java detects the deadlock and throws a DeadlockException
D) One transfer is rolled back automatically by the JVM
assessment.explanation: T1 acquires Lock-A and waits for Lock-B; T2 acquires Lock-B and waits for Lock-A. Neither lock is ever released — this is a classic circular wait deadlock. The JVM does not automatically resolve deadlocks (unlike database engines); threads remain blocked until the application is restarted or a timeout is used.

assessment.text: Why does acquiring locks in account ID order prevent deadlock?
options: A) Because it makes lock acquisition faster by reducing contention
B) Because it eliminates the circular wait condition — all threads acquire locks in the same global order, so no cycle can form
C) Because String.compareTo() is atomic and prevents race conditions
D) Because the JVM guarantees that lexicographically ordered locks are acquired atomically
assessment.explanation: Deadlock requires a circular wait: T1 holds resource A and waits for B, while T2 holds B and waits for A. If all threads always acquire locks in the same global order (e.g., lower ID first), no thread can hold a lock that another thread is waiting for before acquiring the lock the first thread wants — the cycle cannot form.

assessment.text: Which monitoring approach most reliably detects a production deadlock within seconds of occurrence?
options: A) Checking HTTP error rate dashboards for 500s
B) Polling ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() on a scheduled background thread and alerting when count > 0
C) Reviewing logs manually every 5 minutes
D) Setting a database connection pool timeout
assessment.explanation: ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() directly queries the JVM's lock management subsystem and returns the thread IDs involved in a deadlock cycle within milliseconds. Polling it every 5-10 seconds on a watchdog thread provides near-real-time deadlock detection. HTTP error rates and logs are lagging indicators that only surface after customers are already impacted.

experiments.title: Livelock in Payment Retry Loop
experiments.subtitle: Two payment processors repeatedly collide and back off simultaneously, making no progress
experiments.scenario: A payment processing cluster runs two processor instances competing to acquire a distributed advisory lock before processing a pending payment batch. When the lock is unavailable, each processor catches the failure, waits a fixed delay, and retries. Because both processors start at nearly the same time and use the same fixed back-off interval, they perpetually retry in lockstep — each waking up to find the other has just reacquired the resource.
experiments.impact: No payment batches are processed despite both processors being fully healthy and runnable. The livelock is invisible to basic health checks (threads are RUNNABLE, not BLOCKED), causing payment settlement delays that compound over time. Without jitter, the problem worsens under higher concurrency as more processors join the collision pattern.
incorrectCode: public void process(String batchId) throws InterruptedException {

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: fixed delay means all competing threads wake up at the same time and collide again
UNSAFE: identical backoff for all threads — no jitter means all threads retry simultaneously, perpetuating livelock

experiments.failureExplanation: Both processor threads call process() at the same time. One acquires the lock; the other catches LockUnavailableException and sleeps 500ms. The first processor finishes quickly and releases the lock. The second processor wakes up, acquires the lock — but by this time the first processor has also looped back and collides again. With a fixed 500ms delay and near-identical processing times, the two processors synchronize their retry cycles and repeatedly deny each other the lock indefinitely.

simulation.title: Livelock: Fixed Backoff Causes Perpetual Collision

buggySteps.note: P1 attempts to acquire lock
P2 attempts to acquire lock at same time
P1 acquires lock
P2 gets LockUnavailableException
P2 sleeps 500ms (fixed delay)
P1 releases lock and immediately retries
P1 reacquires lock
P2 wakes up, retries — lock held by P1 again!
⚠ P2 sleeps 500ms again — livelock perpetuated
P1 releases and loops — same pattern repeats

simulation.bugAnnotation: Fixed retry delay synchronizes both threads' retry cycles, causing perpetual collision with no progress.

safeSteps.note: P2 computes jittered delay: attempt=1, delay=rand(1,2)*100ms = 170ms
P2 wakes up and acquires lock ✓

simulation.safeAnnotation: Randomized jitter desynchronizes retry timing, breaking the collision cycle so processors make progress.

correctCode: public void process(String batchId) throws InterruptedException {
throw new PaymentProcessingException("Max retries exceeded for " + batchId);
experiments.correctExplanation: Exponential backoff doubles the maximum delay window on each attempt, reducing overall retry rate. ThreadLocalRandom jitter ensures two competing threads wake at different times, breaking the lockstep synchronization that causes livelock.

alternatives.name: Redisson distributed lock with watchdog
code: public void process(String batchId) throws InterruptedException {
throw new PaymentProcessingException("Could not acquire lock");
pros: tryLock with a wait timeout handles all backoff logic internally
Watchdog thread auto-extends lease to prevent expiry during long processing
Redis-backed — works across multiple JVM instances
cons: Redisson client adds latency for every lock operation (network round trip)
alternatives.whenToUse: Use Redisson when the payment service runs in a multi-instance cluster and a distributed lock backed by Redis is already part of the infrastructure.

experiments.performanceNotes: Exponential backoff with jitter is the standard algorithm (AWS uses it for all SDK retries). The key insight is that jitter should be full — randomize the entire interval, not just add a small random delta to a fixed value. Full jitter gives the best collision avoidance at the cost of slightly higher average latency per retry.

performanceTable.notes: Network latency per acquire; best for clusters

code: assertTrue(finished, "Livelock: processors did not finish within 5s");
assertTrue(processed.get() >= 1, "At least one processor must succeed");
tests.explanation: Two processor threads compete for the same batch lock. The test asserts that at least one processor completes within 5 seconds. If the fixed-delay livelock is present, neither thread completes and the CountDownLatch times out, failing the assertion.
tests.limitations: On a very slow CI machine, even jittered backoff may exceed 5 seconds with MAX_ATTEMPTS=10. Tune the timeout or reduce MAX_ATTEMPTS in the test fixture for fast CI environments.

monitoringSymptoms: Thread CPU usage is non-zero (threads are RUNNABLE) but payment batch processed count stays at zero
Lock acquisition failure rate metric stays consistently high without ever dropping to zero
Payment batch latency grows unboundedly while processor health checks report healthy
Log lines show continuous 'LockUnavailableException' at a perfectly regular interval (the fixed delay)
debugTips: Add structured logging of attempt number and computed jitter delay to verify backoff is actually increasing and randomized
Compare lock acquisition timestamps from two processors — if they are separated by exactly RETRY_DELAY_MS repeatedly, livelock is confirmed
Use a distributed tracing tool (Zipkin, Jaeger) to visualize the retry storm across processor instances
productionRecommendations: Always use full jitter exponential backoff for any retry loop competing for a shared resource
Cap maximum attempts and throw a meaningful exception when exhausted — unbounded retry loops hide livelock in production
Track lock contention rates in Prometheus/Grafana; alert when the acquisition failure rate exceeds 20% over a 1-minute window

assessment.text: What is the key difference between a deadlock and a livelock?
options: A) Deadlock always involves more threads than livelock
B) In deadlock, threads are BLOCKED; in livelock, threads are RUNNABLE but make no progress
C) Livelock only occurs in distributed systems while deadlock is JVM-local
D) Deadlock is detected by the JVM; livelock is not
assessment.explanation: In deadlock, threads are BLOCKED waiting for a lock and consume no CPU. In livelock, threads are RUNNABLE — they actively retry, sleep, and retry — but are caught in a pattern where none ever achieves its goal. This makes livelock harder to detect because health checks see active, non-stuck threads.

assessment.text: Why does adding a fixed delay (Thread.sleep(500)) fail to prevent livelock?
options: A) Because Thread.sleep() is not thread-safe
B) Because a fixed delay causes all competing threads to wake up at the same time and collide again
C) Because 500ms is too short a delay for payment processing
D) Because Thread.sleep() does not release held locks
assessment.explanation: If all threads use the same fixed delay and start at nearly the same time, they will sleep for 500ms, wake up together, and collide again on the lock — perpetuating the lockstep cycle. The fix is randomized jitter that desynchronizes wake-up times.

assessment.text: In the full-jitter exponential backoff formula `long cap = BASE * (1L << attempt); long jitter = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, cap + 1)`, what does the `1L << attempt` expression do?
options: A) It divides the base delay by the attempt number to decrease wait time
B) It doubles the maximum delay window on each attempt (2^attempt)
C) It generates a random seed for ThreadLocalRandom
D) It limits the number of retries to the CPU count
assessment.explanation: 1L << attempt is a left bit shift equivalent to 2^attempt. Combined with BASE_DELAY_MS, it creates a cap that doubles on each retry: 100ms, 200ms, 400ms, 800ms… This exponential growth reduces the retry rate over time, alleviating pressure on the shared resource while jitter prevents synchronized wake-ups.

experiments.title: False Sharing in Payment Throughput
experiments.subtitle: Adjacent volatile fields on the same CPU cache line cause cross-core invalidations and 3-4x throughput loss
experiments.scenario: A high-frequency payment processing engine maintains per-processor success and failure counters in a shared PaymentStats object. Each counter is updated by a separate CPU core. Performance profiling shows the payment throughput is 3x lower than the theoretical hardware limit. CPU performance counters reveal an unusually high rate of L1/L2 cache-line invalidations. The two counters are declared adjacent in the class, placing them on the same 64-byte CPU cache line.
experiments.impact: Every time Core 1 increments successCount, it invalidates the cache line on Core 2 — even though Core 2 only uses failureCount. Core 2 must fetch the cache line from Core 1 (or L3/RAM) before it can write, adding dozens of nanoseconds per update. At 10M+ operations per second, this serializes updates that should be fully parallel, cutting throughput by 60-75%.

incorrectAnnotations.note: PERF: successCount and failureCount are adjacent in memory — they share a 64-byte CPU cache line
PERF: writes to failureCount invalidate the cache line that holds successCount on other cores, and vice versa
UNSAFE: volatile++ is not atomic — it is a read-modify-write; use AtomicLong or LongAdder for correctness
UNSAFE: same non-atomic increment issue on failureCount

experiments.failureExplanation: Modern CPUs transfer memory in 64-byte cache lines. When Core 1 writes successCount and Core 2 writes failureCount, both cores hold the same cache line in MODIFIED state. The MESI protocol forces each write to invalidate the other core's copy, requiring a cache-line bounce through L3 (or main memory) before the next write. This false sharing serializes what should be two fully independent counter updates, reducing throughput by 3-4x. Note that volatile++ is also not atomic — false sharing is a performance bug, but the non-atomic increment is a correctness bug.

simulation.title: False Sharing: Cache-Line Ping-Pong Between CPU Cores

buggySteps.note: Core-1 writes successCount — takes ownership of cache line
⚠ Core-2 must fetch invalidated cache line from Core-1 (L3 bounce)
Core-2 writes failureCount — takes ownership of cache line
⚠ Core-1 must fetch invalidated cache line from Core-2 (L3 bounce)
⚠ Writes serialized by cache-line contention, not by logic

simulation.bugAnnotation: Adjacent fields share one cache line; every write by one core forces the other core to reload — serializing logically independent updates.

safeSteps.note: Core-1 writes successCount — cache line held exclusively by Core-1
Core-2 writes failureCount — different cache line, no invalidation ✓
Core-1 writes again — no cache-line bounce ✓

simulation.safeAnnotation: @Contended pads each field to its own 64-byte cache line, allowing cores to update them without interfering with each other.

correctCode: private final LongAdder successCount = new LongAdder();
private final LongAdder failureCount = new LongAdder();
experiments.correctExplanation: @Contended inserts 128 bytes of padding around the annotated field (requires JVM flag -XX:-RestrictContended), placing each counter on its own cache line and preventing cross-core invalidations. LongAdder also provides atomic, high-throughput increment via cell striping.

alternatives.name: Manual padding with long fields
code: public final AtomicLong successCount = new AtomicLong(0);
public long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7;
public final AtomicLong failureCount = new AtomicLong(0);
public long q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6, q7;
pros: No JVM flag required — works out of the box
cons: Fragile: JVM may reorder fields; object layout is not guaranteed
Verbose and easy to get wrong (must pad to 64-byte boundaries)
alternatives.whenToUse: Use manual padding only when @Contended is unavailable (e.g., older JDK without jdk.internal.vm.annotation) and you can verify the layout with a tool like JOL (Java Object Layout).

experiments.performanceNotes: False sharing is a hardware-level performance issue — the fix is purely structural (field layout) and adds no algorithmic complexity. @Contended is the idiomatic Java solution but requires the JVM flag -XX:-RestrictContended to be effective outside the JDK itself. LongAdder provides additional throughput improvement under high contention by striping updates across internal cells.

tests.explanation: JMH runs recordSuccess and recordFailure concurrently with 4 threads (2 per method). The throughput gap between buggy (adjacent fields) and fixed (@Contended) will show the false-sharing penalty. Run with: java -XX:-RestrictContended -jar benchmarks.jar FalseSharingBenchmark.
tests.limitations: JMH results are sensitive to CPU topology. Run on a multi-core machine with NUMA awareness off; pinning threads to separate physical cores maximizes the visible false-sharing effect.

monitoringSymptoms: Payment processing throughput plateaus at 25-35% of hardware-theoretical maximum despite low CPU utilization
CPU performance counters (perf stat) show unusually high LLC-load-misses and cache-line invalidation events
Throughput does not scale linearly when adding more threads — may even decrease beyond 2 threads
Flame graph shows time concentrated in memory barrier instructions (LOCK XADD, MFENCE) rather than business logic
debugTips: Use `perf stat -e cache-misses,cache-references,LLC-load-misses ./myapp` to measure cache pressure — false sharing dramatically increases cache-miss rate
Use Java Object Layout (JOL) tool to inspect field offsets and verify @Contended padding is applied: `ClassLayout.parseClass(PaymentStats.class).toPrintable()`
Compare throughput with -XX:-RestrictContended vs without it — if throughput doubles with the flag, false sharing is confirmed
productionRecommendations: Add -XX:-RestrictContended to JVM startup flags whenever @Contended is used in application code (without it, padding is only applied within the JDK itself)
Prefer LongAdder over volatile long for high-throughput metrics — it handles both atomicity and false sharing via built-in cell striping
Use Micrometer metrics backed by LongAdder for all payment statistics rather than raw fields in shared objects

assessment.text: Why does writing to `failureCount` on Core 2 impact the performance of writing `successCount` on Core 1, even though they are independent fields?
options: A) Because volatile fields use a global lock that serializes all writes
B) Because both fields fit on the same 64-byte CPU cache line, and a write to one invalidates the other core's copy of the entire line
C) Because Java's memory model requires all volatile writes to be visible to all threads immediately
D) Because the JVM merges consecutive volatile writes into a single operation
assessment.explanation: CPUs exchange memory in 64-byte cache lines. When Core 2 writes failureCount, it must take exclusive ownership of the cache line — invalidating Core 1's cached copy of the same line. Core 1 must then reload the line before its next write to successCount. This cache-line bounce adds ~100ns per operation and serializes logically independent updates.

assessment.text: What JVM flag is required for @Contended to pad fields in application code (outside the JDK)?
options: A) -XX:+UseContendedPadding
B) -XX:-RestrictContended
C) -Djava.util.concurrent.padding=true
D) -XX:ContendedPaddingWidth=128
assessment.explanation: -XX:-RestrictContended removes the restriction that limits @Contended's effect to JDK-internal classes. Without this flag, @Contended annotations in user code are silently ignored and no padding is applied. The default padding width is 128 bytes (two cache lines) to protect against adjacent-line prefetch effects.

assessment.text: In the buggy code, `successCount++` on a volatile long is both a correctness bug and a performance bug. Which statement correctly describes both issues?
options: A) It is correct but slow because volatile flushes the entire CPU cache
B) The ++ is not atomic (read-modify-write race) and the adjacent field causes false sharing — fix both with @Contended + LongAdder
C) It is atomic on x86 but not on ARM; use synchronized for portability
D) volatile++ is atomic only when the JVM is in server mode (-server flag)
assessment.explanation: volatile guarantees visibility (writes are immediately visible to other threads) but not atomicity. The ++ operator compiles to a read, increment, and write — three separate operations that another thread can interleave. This is a correctness bug. Additionally, adjacent volatile fields on the same cache line cause false sharing, the performance bug. @Contended fixes false sharing and LongAdder fixes atomicity.

experiments.title: ABA Problem in Lock-Free Balance Update
experiments.subtitle: CAS succeeds on a stale read when value returns to original, allowing a corrupted balance update
experiments.scenario: A high-performance payment ledger uses lock-free balance management with AtomicReference<BigDecimal> and compare-and-set to avoid lock contention. A thread reads the current balance, computes a new value, and uses CAS to update atomically. The issue arises when a preempted thread resumes after the balance has cycled through two intermediate values back to the original — CAS cannot distinguish the original value from the returned value, so the stale update is applied.
experiments.impact: A payment thread reads balance=1000, is preempted while another thread debits 500 (balance=500) and a third thread credits 500 back (balance=1000). The first thread resumes, its CAS of 1000→800 succeeds — but the intermediate 500 debit was based on a different business transaction. The final balance is incorrect and the debit is effectively reversed without any reconciliation, creating an invisible ledger discrepancy.

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: reads current balance — may be preempted here
UNSAFE: CAS checks only the value, not version — if balance cycled A→B→A while preempted, this CAS succeeds incorrectly on stale data

experiments.failureExplanation: Compare-and-set only compares the current value against the expected value. If Thread 1 reads balance=1000 and is preempted, Thread 2 debits 500 (balance=500), Thread 3 credits 500 (balance=1000), and Thread 1 resumes — Thread 1's CAS(1000, 800) succeeds because the current value is still 1000. However, Thread 1's decision (debit 200) was made based on a balance that underwent two intervening transactions. The intermediate state changes are invisible to Thread 1's CAS, constituting the ABA problem.

simulation.title: ABA Problem: Stale CAS Succeeds After Value Cycles Back

buggySteps.note: T1 reads balance = 1000
T1 computes next = 1000 - 200 = 800
T1 preempted before CAS
T2 CAS: 500 → 1000 (credit 500 — balance is back!)
⚠ T1 CAS: 1000 → 800 SUCCEEDS — but balance was 1000 for a different reason!
⚠ T1 returns true; two intermediate transactions are invisible

experiments.correctExplanation: AtomicStampedReference pairs the value with an integer version stamp. CAS must match both the value and the stamp — even if balance returns to its original value, the stamp will have been incremented by intervening operations, causing the stale CAS to fail and triggering a fresh read-and-retry.

alternatives.name: AtomicMarkableReference (boolean flag)
pros: Useful when you only need to detect one specific state change (e.g., logical deletion in a linked list)
Smaller than AtomicStampedReference (one boolean vs integer stamp)
cons: Only one bit of version state — cannot distinguish more than one intervening change
Does not fully solve the general ABA problem; only prevents the specific case where marked=false→true→false
alternatives.whenToUse: Use AtomicMarkableReference when implementing lock-free data structures where logical deletion must be detected (e.g., concurrent linked list node removal), not for financial balance management.

experiments.performanceNotes: AtomicStampedReference is slightly slower than AtomicReference due to the extra stamp comparison in CAS. For financial ledgers, the correctness guarantee is mandatory — the performance cost is negligible compared to the risk of silent balance corruption. Consider using database optimistic locking (JPA @Version) for persistent ledgers, which provides the same ABA protection with transaction rollback semantics.

The FORBIDDEN outcome (true = CAS succeeded with stale snapshot after ABA cycle) demonstrates the bug. With AtomicStampedReference, this outcome becomes impossible.

To trigger the ABA problem here, the cycler must return the exact same BigDecimal object — in practice, `new BigDecimal("1000")` creates different references. Use a wrapper object or Integer for jcstress reproduction; in production, BigDecimal instances from the same value cache can trigger real ABA.

assessment.text: Thread 1 reads balance=1000. Thread 2 changes balance 1000→500→1000. Thread 1 performs CAS(1000, 800). What happens with plain AtomicReference?
options: A) The CAS fails because the reference has changed
B) The CAS succeeds, setting balance to 800 — the two intermediate changes are invisible
C) The CAS throws a ConcurrentModificationException
D) The CAS succeeds only if Thread 2 used synchronized
assessment.explanation: AtomicReference.compareAndSet compares only the current value against the expected value. If the value is back to 1000, the CAS succeeds regardless of any intermediate changes. Thread 1's update is based on stale context, constituting the ABA problem. Java provides no mechanism to detect this with plain AtomicReference.

assessment.text: How does AtomicStampedReference solve the ABA problem?
options: A) It uses a synchronized lock internally to prevent concurrent modifications
B) It pairs the value with an integer version stamp; CAS must match both value and stamp — incremented stamps reveal ABA cycles
C) It compares object identity instead of value equality, preventing reuse of old values
D) It stores a copy of all previous values and rejects writes that match any historical value
assessment.explanation: AtomicStampedReference stores a (value, stamp) pair. Each successful CAS increments the stamp. Even if the value returns to its original (1000), the stamp will be higher than the snapshot taken before the ABA cycle, causing the stale thread's CAS to fail and forcing a fresh read with the current state.

assessment.text: In production financial systems, what is generally the preferred mechanism for preventing ABA-style issues in balance updates?
options: A) Using AtomicReference with a very short retry timeout
B) Database-level optimistic locking with a @Version column, backed by UPDATE WHERE version=? semantics
C) Adding a Thread.sleep() between reads and writes to reduce collision probability
D) Using double-checked locking with volatile
assessment.explanation: Database optimistic locking (@Version in JPA, or WHERE version=? in raw SQL) provides ABA protection at the persistence layer with full ACID semantics, audit trail, and automatic rollback on conflict. It is more reliable than in-memory CAS for financial balances because it survives application restarts, handles distributed services, and integrates with transaction management.

experiments.title: Thread Pool Starvation Under Burst Load
experiments.subtitle: Blocking I/O inside a fixed thread pool exhausts all threads, queuing subsequent requests until timeout
experiments.scenario: A payment authorization service uses a fixed thread pool of 10 threads to handle incoming payment requests. Each authorization must call a downstream KYC (Know Your Customer) compliance service over HTTP before returning a result. The KYC service has variable latency (50-500ms). Under normal load, the 10 threads are sufficient. During flash sale events, payment volume spikes and all 10 threads block on KYC HTTP calls simultaneously. New requests queue up, hit their HTTP timeout, and are rejected — even though the payment service CPU usage is near zero.
experiments.impact: During a 30-second burst with 50 concurrent payment requests, all 10 thread pool threads block on KYC calls. The 40 queued requests time out, generating customer-visible payment failures and revenue loss. The service reports 80% error rate despite being entirely healthy — the issue is pool exhaustion from blocking I/O, not any application logic error.

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: fixed pool of 10 — if all 10 threads block on I/O, no new tasks can run
UNSAFE: kycClient.check() is a blocking HTTP call — this thread blocks for 50-500ms while holding a pool thread

experiments.failureExplanation: A fixed thread pool of size N can only handle N concurrent tasks regardless of whether they are blocked on I/O or doing actual work. kycClient.check() blocks the thread for the duration of the HTTP request (50-500ms). With 10 threads and >10 concurrent payment requests, the 11th through Nth requests queue in the executor's internal queue. If the queue is bounded or timeout is applied upstream, requests are rejected. The pool is not 'busy' in the CPU sense — all 10 threads are simply sleeping, waiting for HTTP responses.

experiments.correctExplanation: Separating fast-path (non-blocking) and KYC blocking-I/O work into dedicated thread pools ensures that slow KYC calls cannot exhaust the threads serving other payment logic. The KYC pool is sized for the expected blocking concurrency and monitored independently.

alternatives.name: Java 21 Virtual Threads
pros: Virtual threads are extremely lightweight (KB of stack vs MB for platform threads)
Blocking I/O on a virtual thread yields the carrier thread automatically — no pool starvation
Dramatically simplifies code — no pool tuning or separate executors needed
cons: synchronized blocks inside KYC client may pin virtual threads (see java-02 experiment)
Requires Java 21; available as preview in Java 19/20
Unbounded virtual thread creation needs rate limiting to prevent OOM from millions of pending tasks
alternatives.whenToUse: Use virtual threads on Java 21+ when the workload is primarily I/O-bound and the HTTP client / JDBC driver does not use synchronized internally (or has been updated to use ReentrantLock).

experiments.performanceNotes: Thread pool sizing for I/O-bound work follows Little's Law: N = λ × W, where λ is arrival rate (tasks/sec) and W is average wait time (seconds). For 100 KYC calls/sec with 200ms average latency, you need N = 100 × 0.2 = 20 threads minimum. Add 50% headroom. Virtual threads eliminate this calculation entirely for I/O-bound tasks.

No pool starvation; JVM manages scheduling

The buggy fixed-10-thread pool will only process 10 concurrently; the other 10 queue and each takes >2s, so the total time exceeds 4s and the 5s countdown fails. The fixed version using a separate KYC pool processes all 20 within 2-3s.
tests.limitations: The test uses a mock KYC client with Thread.sleep, which simulates blocking I/O at the Java thread level. In a real integration test with Testcontainers and an actual HTTP stub server, verify that pool active thread count metrics stay below the KYC pool size limit.

monitoringSymptoms: Payment authorization error rate spikes during traffic bursts while CPU utilization remains below 20%
Thread pool active thread count stays at max-pool-size for extended periods during bursts
JVM thread dump shows all pool threads in TIMED_WAITING state blocked on HTTP socket read
Executor queue size metric grows linearly during the burst then drops to zero as the burst ends
debugTips: Export ThreadPoolExecutor getActiveCount() and getQueue().size() as Micrometer gauges to detect saturation in real time
Take a thread dump during a burst: if all threads show the same KYC HTTP call stack, starvation is confirmed
Use -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full (Java 21) if migrating to virtual threads — synchronization inside the HTTP client may pin threads and negate the benefit
productionRecommendations: Size thread pools using Little's Law for I/O-bound tasks: N = arrival_rate × average_latency, with 50% headroom
Always separate CPU-bound and I/O-bound work into different executor pools; monitor each pool independently
On Java 21, prefer virtual threads with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() for I/O-bound tasks — eliminates pool sizing guesswork entirely

assessment.text: With a fixed pool of 10 threads and a KYC call that takes 200ms on average, what is the maximum payment authorization throughput?
options: A) Unlimited — thread pools scale automatically
B) 50 payments/second (10 threads × 1000ms/200ms)
C) 10 payments/second (pool size limits concurrency)
D) 200 payments/second (10 threads × 20 cycles/sec)
assessment.explanation: With 10 threads each taking 200ms per KYC call, each thread can handle 1000/200 = 5 calls per second. 10 threads × 5 calls/sec = 50 payments/second maximum throughput. Beyond this rate, the pool is saturated and additional requests queue or timeout.

assessment.text: Why does Java 21 virtual threads solve thread pool starvation for I/O-bound workloads?
options: A) Virtual threads use a larger stack size, allowing more I/O operations
B) When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from the carrier thread, freeing the carrier to run other virtual threads
C) Virtual threads run in a separate JVM process and don't share the thread pool
D) Virtual threads make all I/O operations asynchronous automatically
assessment.explanation: Virtual threads (Java 21) are managed by the JVM scheduler. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O (socket read, JDBC query), the JVM 'parks' it and mounts a different virtual thread on the same carrier thread. This means thousands of virtual threads can be active concurrently with only a handful of carrier threads — I/O blocking no longer holds a carrier thread.

assessment.text: Which monitoring signal most reliably indicates thread pool starvation rather than a legitimate traffic spike?
options: A) High HTTP 500 error rate
B) CPU utilization near 100%
C) Thread pool active count at maximum while queue size grows and CPU utilization is low
D) High garbage collection pause times
assessment.explanation: Thread pool starvation is characterized by all threads being occupied (active count = max) while CPU utilization is low — the threads are blocked waiting for I/O, not computing. A growing queue confirms incoming requests are waiting for a free thread. High CPU + high error rate would suggest actual overload. Low CPU + max active threads is the starvation signature.

experiments.title: Unsafe Publication of Configuration Object
experiments.subtitle: Without volatile, threads may observe a partially initialized config object due to instruction reordering
experiments.scenario: A payment processing service loads its configuration (rate limits, merchant rules, feature flags) from a database at startup and publishes it to all processing threads via a static field. The configuration is re-loaded periodically to pick up rule changes. Because the static field is not volatile and the configuration object is not immutable, the Java Memory Model permits publishing threads to see instance != null while the internal fields (rules, limits, flags) are still null or zero — a partially initialized object.
experiments.impact: A processing thread reads instance != null and proceeds to call instance.getRules().get(merchantId) — but rules is still null because the JVM reordered the constructor's field assignments after the assignment to instance. This causes NullPointerException in the payment critical path, or silently applies empty rules, allowing payments to bypass fraud checks. The bug is non-reproducible in development (single-core laptops rarely reorder) and only surfaces under heavy multi-core production load.
incorrectCode: public static void init(Map<String,String> r, Map<String,Integer> limits) {
public Map<String, String> getRules()      { return rules; }
public Map<String, Integer> getRateLimits() { return rateLimits; }

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: instance is not volatile — writes to it are not guaranteed to be visible in order to other threads
UNSAFE: cfg.rules assigned inside constructor — the JVM may reorder this after the assignment to instance on line 17
UNSAFE: cfg.rateLimits assignment may also be reordered past the instance publication
UNSAFE: instance = cfg may be observed by another thread before rules/rateLimits are written (partial init)

experiments.failureExplanation: The Java Memory Model permits the JIT compiler and CPU to reorder stores to cfg.rules and cfg.rateLimits relative to the store to instance, as long as the result is correct within a single thread. A reading thread may see the new non-null reference in instance but then observe null for rules or rateLimits because those stores have not yet propagated. Without a happens-before relationship (established by volatile, final fields in constructors, or synchronized), the reading thread has no guarantee about the order of these writes.

public Map<String, String>  getRules()      { return rules; }
public Map<String, Integer> getRateLimits() { return rateLimits; }
experiments.correctExplanation: Declaring instance volatile establishes a happens-before relationship: all writes completed before the volatile store (including final field initialization inside the constructor) are visible to any thread that reads the volatile field. Making fields final and assigning them in the constructor provides an additional JMM guarantee: fully constructed objects with final fields are safely published regardless of the reference publication mechanism.

pros: Class loading guarantees safe publication — no volatile needed
Lazy initialization: config is not loaded until first access
Thread-safe by JVM specification without any synchronization overhead
cons: Config is initialized only once — cannot be reloaded at runtime
If config needs periodic refresh, the Holder idiom must be replaced with volatile or AtomicReference
alternatives.whenToUse: Use the Holder idiom for truly immutable, load-once configuration. Use volatile AtomicReference for configuration that must be refreshable at runtime.

experiments.performanceNotes: volatile reads have negligible overhead on modern x86 (a load fence). The happens-before guarantee of volatile is exactly what is needed for safe publication — it does not introduce lock contention. For read-heavy configuration access (many threads, infrequent writes), volatile is the ideal mechanism: zero contention on reads, full visibility guarantee on writes.

Consider using Spring's @RefreshScope with an AtomicReference<ConfigSnapshot> for runtime-refreshable configuration, which makes the publish-swap operation explicit and observable

assessment.text: Why can a reading thread see instance != null but rules == null in the buggy code?
options: A) Because HashMap is not thread-safe and clears itself under load
B) Because the JIT compiler and CPU may reorder the store to instance before the stores to cfg.rules and cfg.rateLimits
C) Because static fields are initialized lazily and may not be ready on first access
D) Because Java always clears object fields to null between constructor calls
assessment.explanation: The Java Memory Model allows the JIT and CPU to reorder independent stores within a thread as long as the single-thread result is preserved. The store to instance and the stores to cfg.rules are independent from the JVM's perspective. Without a happens-before guarantee (from volatile, synchronized, or final fields in constructor), other threads may observe the non-null instance reference before the rules assignment is visible.

assessment.text: How does adding volatile to the instance field fix the unsafe publication?
options: A) volatile prevents the JVM from ever reordering any stores within the JVM
B) A volatile write inserts a memory fence that ensures all preceding writes are visible to any thread that subsequently reads the volatile field
C) volatile makes the entire PaymentConfig object immutable
D) volatile forces the JVM to serialize all accesses to the instance field
assessment.explanation: A volatile write inserts a StoreStore memory barrier before the write and a StoreLoad barrier after, ensuring that all stores that happened before the volatile write (including cfg.rules and cfg.rateLimits assignments) are flushed and visible. Any thread that reads the volatile instance field is guaranteed to see all writes that preceded the volatile store — establishing a happens-before relationship.

assessment.text: Why is this bug more likely to manifest on AWS Graviton (ARM) than on x86 development machines?
options: A) ARM processors are slower and have less memory bandwidth
B) The x86 Total Store Order (TSO) memory model is stronger than ARM's relaxed model — TSO prevents many store reorderings that ARM explicitly allows
C) AWS Graviton uses a different JVM version that has different volatile semantics
D) ARM processors do not support the volatile keyword
assessment.explanation: x86 uses Total Store Order (TSO), which prohibits store-store reordering — coincidentally making many unsafe publications 'work' on x86. ARM uses a weaker memory model that explicitly allows store-store reordering unless memory barriers are inserted. Code that is technically incorrect per the Java Memory Model often appears to work on x86 but fails on ARM, making ARM-based cloud instances (AWS Graviton, Apple M-series) valuable for catching JMM violations.
